content:
"Northern Territory police faced severe criticism from Coroner Greg Cavanagh after failing to address repeated incidents of self-harm and suicide attempts in caged police vehicles, ultimately leading to the tragic death of 23-year-old Dale Scott Walkinshaw. The coroner’s report revealed that despite an internal recommendation in 2013 to install CCTV cameras following a prior death in custody, police had taken no action. Shockingly, in the three years between the two fatalities, there were at least 16 attempted suicides in these vehicles, with six victims only discovered when they were semi-conscious or unconscious.

Cavanagh’s damning assessment concluded that it was not a question of *if* someone would die in the back of a police van, but *when.*

The chain of events leading to Walkinshaw’s death began on the night of September 16. Two officers, en route to a noise complaint in Darwin, stumbled upon the aftermath of a violent crash. A Toyota Hilux had veered off the Stuart Highway, slamming into a palm tree near Bargot Road, close to the airport. Behind the wreckage, concealed by vegetation, they found Walkinshaw—physically unhurt but cradling his badly injured passenger, a young woman he’d met earlier that evening at a bar. She was drifting in and out of consciousness, her back severely injured. Walkinshaw, reeking of alcohol, blew a blood alcohol level of 0.149—nearly three times the legal limit.

What happened next would expose the systemic failures already identified by the coroner. Walkinshaw was placed in the caged compartment of a police van, where, left unmonitored, he attempted to take his own life. By the time officers checked on him, it was too late. The tragedy underscored the coroner’s grim prediction and left a community in mourning, demanding answers about how a preventable death had been allowed to occur twice."
